title: Gaudete Sunday (Philippians 4:4)
hookLine: the rose candle: rejoice, the Lord is near

cards: Look at an Advent wreath in its third week. Two purple candles have burned down a little. Then there's one that isn't purple at all.
It's pink, or as the Church calls it, rose. On the third Sunday of Advent the priest may wear rose vestments too, a color that appears only twice a year.
People who don't know why sometimes think the florist got the order wrong. The real reason is one Latin word, the first word sung at that Sunday's Mass for many centuries.

teach.b: Gaudete means rejoice, said to more than one person. It opens the entrance chant of the third Sunday of Advent, taken from Paul's letter to the Philippians.
In the Douay-Rheims: "Rejoice in the Lord always; again, I say, rejoice." The reason follows a verse later: "The Lord is nigh." Here's what gives it weight.
Paul wrote this letter in chains. He mentions his bonds again and again, and he isn't sure he'll leave prison alive. So this isn't a cheerful man telling everyone to smile.
It's a prisoner insisting that joy has a source outside his circumstances. Advent is a season of waiting, and waiting can turn grim. So halfway through, the Church lightens the color.
Purple softens to rose, like the first light of dawn at the edge of the sky. It isn't Christmas yet; the waiting isn't over. But the nearness has started to show.

teach.h: A WEEK OF ADVENT, LOOKED BACK.
teach.b: Gaudete Sunday ends a week that has walked a long way. It opened with the Bible's last prayer, maranatha, take the water of life, freely. Then, every day has a rank.
The new year began with one word, watch.
Isaiah gave a great light. Kecharitomene gave full of grace from the start. Guadalupe gave am I not here.
And now rose, and rejoice. Read in a row, they make a small Advent of their own: a cry, a calendar, a lookout, a light, a girl, a mother, and joy on the way.

how: On the third Sunday of Advent many Catholic parishes light the rose candle of the Advent wreath, and the priest may wear rose vestments instead of violet.

o: Latin: the rose color worn by the priest
Latin: wait, said during a quiet season
Latin: rejoice, said to a whole crowd

s: the pink candle is a florist's mistake
it's rose, for Gaudete Sunday, the third Sunday of Advent.
Paul wrote rejoice in the Lord always from prison
he speaks of his bonds throughout the letter.
rose vestments mean the waiting is over
Christmas hasn't come. the color softens because the nearness has begun to show.

games.q: you're Paul, in chains, unsure you'll leave prison alive. you're writing to friends in Philippi. what do you tell them?
o: to rejoice in the Lord always.
to come and break you out.
games.why: rejoice in the Lord always; again, I say, rejoice. the Lord is nigh. joy with a source outside his circumstances.

practice: If you can, put on one bright thing before you sit, a scarf, socks, a ring, the pink shirt you never wear, and sit with it on.

Name one honest reason for joy today, even small, even beside something hard, the way Paul found his in chains, without forcing a feeling. If you pray, say Paul's words, rejoice in the Lord always; if not, let the color remind you.

wordCard.voice: Gaudete. Latin for rejoice, said to many. It names the third Sunday of Advent, with its rose candle and rose vestments. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: rejoice (to many), the first word of the entrance chant for the third Sunday of Advent.

carryVoice: Your line: rejoice. Joy can come even in chains, because the Lord is nigh. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: Rejoice in the Lord always; again, I say, rejoice.
